elements.quote: We searched PubMed, Scopus, APA PsycInfo, and eight peer-reviewed journals to identify cancer-related studies that used system dynamics modeling. A dual review process was used to determine eligibility.
elements.reason: The abstract describes a systematic search and dual review process and reports included studies, but does not explicitly label the report as a 'systematic review' in the abstract text.

elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states the review objective: to determine the breadth, characteristics, and quality of system dynamics studies applied to cancer prevention and control.

elements.quote: System dynamics modeling can illustrate complex interactions and help identify potential interventions across the cancer control continuum. Prior efforts have been hampered by a lack of rigor and transparency regarding model development and testing. Supportive infrastructure for increasing awareness, accessibility, and further development of best practices of system dynamics for multidisciplinary cancer research is needed.

elements.quote: Cancer is a complex, multilevel phenomenon [1-5] in which health outcomes depend on highly interrelated elements across stages of etiology, prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment, survivorship, and end-of-life care [6, 7]. Standard bench and clinical research approaches alone are not well suited to account for this complexity, as most cancer control interventions often focus on explicit, often linear health outcomes of a specific, well-defined population [1, 8, 9]. ... Although system dynamics modeling has been utilized in various aspects of public health since the 1970s, past reviews in this field have noted a significant increase in their use since the early 2000s, especially in areas focused on chronic or non-communicable diseases [24, 25]. The extent to which system dynamics modeling has been applied specifically to cancer prevention and control has not been studied.
elements.reason: The introduction summarizes the current state of knowledge about complexity in cancer and use of system dynamics in public health, cites past reviews noting increases, and explicitly identifies the gap (extent of application to cancer prevention/control has not been studied).

elements.quote: In a 2019 report, the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine argued that systems science methods could help illustrate the multilevel nature of cancer effects and costs to society and help cancer control efforts be more agile and adaptive [7]. The Journal of the National Cancer Institute published several reports calling for the use of complex, multilevel, or systems-focused approaches to advance the landscape of cancer prevention and control [1, 2, 10]. Systems models, particularly well calibrated simulation models, provide a relatively lowcost and low-risk opportunity for comparing potential interventions or treatments in silico before involving busy clinics and patients in trials [1, 7, 11, 12]. ... The extent to which system dynamics modeling has been applied specifically to cancer prevention and control has not been studied.
elements.reason: The authors cite authoritative calls for systems methods and explain the practical benefits of systems models, and then state the specific knowledge gap motivating the review, thereby explaining the importance and need for the review.

elements.quote: Although system dynamics modeling has been utilized in various aspects of public health since the 1970s, past reviews in this field have noted a significant increase in their use since the early 2000s, especially in areas focused on chronic or non-communicable diseases [24, 25]. The extent to which system dynamics modeling has been applied specifically to cancer prevention and control has not been studied.
elements.reason: The manuscript acknowledges previous reviews in the broader field (cites [24,25]) and explains why the current review is needed (those reviews did not assess application specifically to cancer prevention and control).

elements.quote: System dynamics modeling, which consists of diagramming and simulation approaches for understanding and managing such complexity, is being increasingly applied to cancer prevention and control, but the breadth, characteristics, and quality of these studies is not known.

elements.quote: Included articles: 1) were published in peer-reviewed journals; 2) were written in English; 3) used system dynamics modeling (i.e., causal-loop diagramming, stock-and-flow diagramming, or computational system dynamics modeling); 4) pertained to cancer prevention or control; and 4) were published within the last 10 years.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists the study-level eligibility characteristics used to determine inclusion (publication type, language, modeling approach, topical focus, and publication time window).

elements.quote: Included articles: 1) were published in peer-reviewed journals; 2) were written in English; ... and 4) were published within the last 10 years.
elements.reason: Report-level eligibility criteria including publication status (peer-reviewed), language (English), and dissemination year window (last 10 years) are explicitly stated.
No evidence was found distinguishing exclusions because outcomes were not measured from exclusions because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: As shown in Fig 1, most studies included a computational system dynamics simulation model (n = 21; 66%), while the remaining studies (n = 11; 34%) used only diagramming approaches (referred to as diagram-only studies in this review).
elements.reason: The review specifies groups used in synthesis (e.g., simulation vs. diagram-only) and clusters topics, but does not explicitly link these groups to specific comparisons defined in the review objectives (no explicit statement tying groups to predefined comparisons).

elements.quote: In bounding our review to studies published in the last 10 years, we excluded older studies that could have contributed to this synthesis. We also excluded studies related to topics such as nutrition and physical activity if they did not include cancer in their models or research aims. ... Due to our focus on cancer prevention and control, we also excluded studies that were solely related to cancer pathogenesis;
elements.reason: The authors provide rationales for notable restrictions (time window, exclusion of studies not explicitly including cancer such as nutrition/physical activity models, and exclusion of pathogenesis-only studies) and discuss the implications of these restrictions.

elements.quote: Searches for peer-reviewed publications were conducted between February and April 2022 through the PubMed, Scopus, and APA PsycInfo databases using the search terms 'cancer' AND ("causal loop" OR "system dynamics * " OR "systems thinking" OR "group model * "). ... A detailed search strategy can be found in S2 Appendix.
elements.reason: The main text lists databases searched and the exact search string used and explicitly states that a detailed (full) search strategy is provided in S2 Appendix.

elements.quote: To our knowledge, this was the first study to systematically review prior applications of system dynamics modeling across the cancer control continuum. In their review of system dynamics models pertaining to public health and medicine, Darabi and Hosseinichimeh [17] identified a handful of studies using system dynamics modeling to replicate clinical trials and simulate different interventions related to cancer, noting that this area is 'generally underexplored' and would likely benefit from further development of models for cancer screening and treatment. Similar to the findings of our paper, this review found that only a fraction of disease-related modeling studies published their model equations and methodology for development. In a scoping review of system dynamics studies related to addiction, Naumann and colleagues [65] found similarly that the method has been underutilized and that participant engagement should be further used in future studies. In their review of system dynamics models used to assess economic efficiency in public health, Jadeja and colleagues [11] also found underutilization of participatory approaches. In a study of system dynamics applications across business, environment, and health care domains, Zanker and colleagues [27] also found weak verification and validation of models published in articles that provided little or no methodological details outlining model development. These omissions threaten the validity of the specific models being described, as well as the perceived credibility and value of modeling as a method. Stange and colleagues' [1] literature review outlined global observations and opportunities for multilevel interventions across the cancer control continuum. As in our review, the authors noted a greater focus on topics around prevention and screening, as opposed to other areas along the continuum, like cancer survivorship.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly compare their findings to prior reviews and studies, noting consistencies (e.g., underutilization of participatory approaches, limited methodological detail, focus areas) and situating their results within the existing literature.

elements.quote: This study has several limitations. In bounding our review to studies published in the last 10 years, we excluded older studies that could have contributed to this synthesis. We also excluded studies related to topics such as nutrition and physical activity if they did not include cancer in their models or research aims. While we feel this narrowed criteria was helpful in maintaining focus, inclusion of models more tangentially related to cancer might have provided a more comprehensive understanding of the current range of research. Due to our focus on cancer prevention and control, we also excluded studies that were solely related to cancer pathogenesis; if these were included, far more studies would be categorized as relating to etiology in the cancer control continuum. Our understanding of the applications of modeling covered in the included studies was also limited by the descriptions included in the articles themselves, which were shaped by journal audience. Our quality ratings, therefore, reflected both modeling and reporting. Finally, the diversity of model purposes, types, and applications presented a challenge to adapting the quality assessment criteria. While we chose to apply a universal set of criteria to included studies to enable comparison, future research could further specify tailored criteria (e.g., based on model purpose).
elements.reason: The Limitations section explicitly discusses multiple limitations of the evidence included in the review (timeframe restriction, excluded topics/study types, reporting limitations, and heterogeneity affecting quality assessment), directly addressing the checklist item.

elements.quote: Provide a supportive funding environment .                                     | System dynamics modeling is often exploratory in nature, but requires expertise and resources to be done well.
